About.metaDescription: Learn about PickleLlama and our approach to AI and automation consulting.
About.heroSubtitle: We're intentionally small, proudly unconventional (see our mascot), and allergic to corporate theater.
About.storyParagraph1: We started PickleLlama because we wanted to build some cool stuff and make a living. We didn't start out with a grand vision or a plan to change the world. Really, we still don't.
About.storyParagraph2: Most of our early existence as a company was spent working on projects for other companies. We learned a lot about what works and what doesn't. We have some war stories from that era.
About.storyParagraph3: Since then, we have worked for companies of a lot of different sizes and in a lot of different industries from startups to 100 billion dollar giants. Sometimes we even do small projects for friends and family because they have fun ideas.
About.storyParagraph4: We are optimizing for working with
About.storyParagraph4End: and building cool things that solve real problems.
About.storyParagraph4Bold: Ideally, we all make a good living.
About.howWeWorkCard1Text: We'd rather ship something good in two weeks than something perfect in six months. Perfect is the enemy of done.
About.howWeWorkCard2Text: We price based on value delivered, not time spent. Your success is our success.
About.howWeWorkCard3Text: If we can't help you, we'll tell you. We'd rather say no than waste your time and money.
About.howWeWorkCard4Text: We build the simplest thing that could possibly work. Complexity is a liability, not an asset.

Services.metaDescription: How PickleLlama works: understanding first, buy before build, and AI-powered implementation when custom software is the right answer.
Services.heroSubtitle: Over the years, we have watched projects crash and burn. Learning from failure has led us to develop a process we're proud to share. There is a story and a reason behind each step.
Services.heroTagline: These are the steps we find essential for an enjoyable long-term relationship.
Services.step1Description: We listen and produce a report on what we understood
Services.step2Description: We find solutions that don't require hiring us
Services.step3Description: We quantify problems and prioritize by ROI
Services.step4Description: We build, prototype-first, validated with real users
Services.section1Para1: For the first year after starting PickleLlama, we pretty much exclusively worked as subcontractors for other agencies. Probably the most painful lesson we learned in that time was what happens when no one checks with the end user to make sure that the software being built is actually what they need.
Services.section1Para2: One of our projects came to a very sad and frustrating end when, in the last two weeks of the project, we were presented with a checklist of "must haves" from the client that we had never seen before. We tried our best, but in the end, what we built could only do 20% of what we set out to build.
Services.section1Para3: The happy note is that it still recovered hundreds of hours of time every month and allowed their team to focus on more important things. But it could have been so much more if we had only known what the client actually needed.
Services.section1Para4: This story is a big reason why we don't do subcontracting anymore. Client relationships matter too much, and good outcomes are too important.
Services.section1Para5: That's why every engagement starts with understanding. We produce a detailed report on what we heard you say—so we're on the same page before anything else happens.
Services.section1Cta: Learn more about our first meeting
Services.section2Title: Why We Try to Convince You Not to Hire Us
Services.section2Para1: There aren't many new ideas. That's the crushing reality of building a business. With 8 billion people on the planet, it's almost guaranteed that someone else already thought of it. That means you probably shouldn't build it yourself.
Services.section2Para2: Now, you might say, "but you are in the software building business..."
Services.section2Para3: Yes. And here's why we still try to convince you to buy something else first.
Services.section2MathCustomText: Not just to build, but to maintain. A custom solution might cost $50,000-$200,000 to build, plus ongoing maintenance, hosting, security updates, and the inevitable "can you just add this one feature" requests.
Services.section2MathSaasText: A SaaS tool might cost $200-$2,000/month. That's $2,400-$24,000/year. Even at the high end, you'd need to run that tool for 8+ years before you'd have spent what a custom build costs—and you get updates, support, and new features included.
Services.section2WastePara1: We've seen a company spend $150,000 on a custom inventory management system when NetSuite would have done 95% of what they needed for $1,500/month. They spent three years building and maintaining something that a product team of 50 people was already improving every month.
Services.section2WastePara2: We've watched startups burn six months building internal tools that Airtable or Notion could have handled in an afternoon.
Services.section2WastePara3: We don't want to be part of that story. It's bad for you, and honestly, it's not the kind of work we find fulfilling.
Services.section2HurtIntro: Actually, no. Here's what happens when we tell someone they don't need custom software:
Services.section2Reason1Description: When we eventually do recommend building, they know it's because we genuinely believe it's the right call—not because we're trying to generate billable work.
Services.section2Reason2Description: Maybe they don't need custom software today. But when they do have a problem that genuinely requires it, guess who they call?
Services.section2Reason3Description: "These are the people who told me NOT to hire them" is a surprisingly effective endorsement.
Services.section2Reason4Description: When we filter out the projects that shouldn't be custom, what's left are the genuinely interesting, high-impact projects where custom software is the right answer. That's the work we want to do.
Services.section2Summary: We always recommend buying and integrating first, building second. Before we build anything, we exhaustively research options for solving your problems without hiring us.
Services.section2Cta: Learn more about our research report
Services.section3Para1: Most companies have dozens of problems they could throw technology at. The hard part isn't building solutions—it's knowing which problems are worth solving.
Services.section3Para2: We've seen companies spend months building solutions to problems that cost them $10,000/year. That's a bad trade. We've also seen companies ignore problems that were costing them $500,000/year because they didn't realize how much it added up.
Services.section3Para3: Problem identification isn't just listing what's broken. It's quantifying the cost and prioritizing by ROI.
Services.section3LookFor1Description: Where are your people spending hours on tasks that should take minutes?
Services.section3LookFor2Description: Where do mistakes happen most often? What do they cost to fix?
Services.section3LookFor3Description: What's slowing everything else down? What could scale if this was fixed?
Services.section3LookFor4Description: What frustrations are driving good people away? What opportunities are you missing?
Services.section3Summary: We don't just make a list. We put numbers on everything—so you can make informed decisions about what's worth fixing and in what order.
Services.section4Title: When We Build, We Do It Differently
Services.section4Para1: Traditionally, building software has been extremely expensive and time-consuming. Building things in an exploratory fashion to see if they work has been a luxury that even large enterprises frequently couldn't afford.
Services.section4Para2: AI has changed the economics, especially when it comes to prototyping.
Services.section4ValueTitle: The Value of Code: From Caviar to Canned Tuna
Services.section4ValuePara1: Code used to be precious. Every line was expensive to write, expensive to maintain, expensive to change. Companies hoarded code and protected it like treasure.
Services.section4ValuePara2: That's changing. AI makes it possible to generate working prototypes in hours instead of weeks. The value isn't in the code itself anymore—it's in understanding what to build and making sure it actually solves the problem.
Services.section4VulnerabilityTitle: The Real Vulnerability of Custom Software
Services.section4VulnerabilityPara1: Building production-quality software still takes time and effort—less than even two years ago, but it's not trivial. Production systems still have to be reliable, scalable, secure, and usable.
Services.section4VulnerabilityPara2: But the most pressing vulnerability of custom software is actually building the right software.
Services.section4VulnerabilityPara3: We've seen projects where the engineering team delivered extremely high-quality software, only to find out in the last weeks of the project that the software solved the wrong problem—albeit very well.
Services.section4AiPara1: AI doesn't just accelerate building production systems. It allows us to very quickly bootstrap ideas into test articles that prove or disprove our beliefs about the world.
Services.section4AiPara2: We prototype in days. We test with real users. We validate before we invest in production-quality code. This means fewer expensive mistakes and faster time to value.

WhoWeWorkWith.metaDescription: We're selective about who we work with. Learn about the mid-market companies we partner with and whether we're a good fit for your business.
WhoWeWorkWith.heroHeading: We're selective about who we work with. Here's why that's good for you.
WhoWeWorkWith.heroDescription: We don't take on every project that comes through the door. We build long-term technology partnerships with companies whose values align with ours — because the best software comes from genuine collaboration between people who give a damn.
WhoWeWorkWith.pullQuote: We believe the primary purpose of great software is to make the people doing the work happier, more effective, and more able to focus on what they do best.
WhoWeWorkWith.underservedMiddleParagraph1: Mid-market companies — typically between $10M and $100M in revenue — occupy a unique position. You're large enough to have genuinely complex operational challenges, but not so large that you have a 50-person IT department to throw at them. You've outgrown spreadsheets and workarounds, but enterprise software vendors treat you like an afterthought.
WhoWeWorkWith.underservedMiddleParagraph2: That's exactly where we work. We specialize in companies where real operational problems have gone unsolved — not because leadership doesn't care, but because the right solution didn't exist at a reasonable cost. Until recently. Modern AI-augmented development has fundamentally changed what's possible, and problems that used to be too expensive to solve are now very much within reach.
WhoWeWorkWith.valuesHeading: What We Value in a Partner
WhoWeWorkWith.value1Description: We want honest conversations. If something isn't working, say so. If you're not interested, tell us. We'll do the same. The best partnerships are built on trust, not polite fiction.
WhoWeWorkWith.value2Description: You think about how your business runs, not just whether it runs. You're considering where you need to be in two to five years and what it takes to get there.
WhoWeWorkWith.value3Description: You're interested in new ideas and willing to experiment. Not recklessly — you're practical and grounded — but you're open to the possibility that there's a better way.
WhoWeWorkWith.value4Description: You care about your team. You want to give them better tools, not just cut costs. When we take a painful process off someone's plate, that matters to you as much as the efficiency gain.
WhoWeWorkWith.value5Description: You understand that meaningful improvement requires commitment — your time, attention, and budget alongside ours. The best projects are genuine partnerships where both sides show up.
WhoWeWorkWith.value6Description: You've been around. You're not a startup chasing product-market fit — you're an established business looking to modernize, streamline, and prepare for what's next.
WhoWeWorkWith.fitSubheading: A quick self-assessment to save us both time
WhoWeWorkWith.goodFitHeading: We're probably a great fit if…
WhoWeWorkWith.goodFit1: Your team is still managing important processes with spreadsheets, paper forms, or email chains
WhoWeWorkWith.goodFit2: You've been meaning to "do something about technology" but haven't found the right partner

ControversialOpinions.metaDescription: Our contrarian views on software, AI, consulting, and how work should actually get done.
ControversialOpinions.heroDescription: Things we believe that might ruffle some feathers. We're not trying to be contrarian for its own sake—these are hard-won lessons from years of watching projects succeed and fail.
ControversialOpinions.opinion1Title: Most AI Projects Shouldn't Be Built
ControversialOpinions.opinion1Paragraph1: We make money building AI solutions, but we'll be the first to tell you that most AI projects are solutions looking for problems. Before you automate something, make sure it's actually worth automating. (Or possible to automate.)
ControversialOpinions.opinion1Paragraph2: Sometimes a spreadsheet, a checklist, or just hiring another person is the right answer. We'd rather lose a project than build something that doesn't deliver real value.
ControversialOpinions.opinion2Title: Outcome is the only thing that matters.
ControversialOpinions.opinion2Paragraph1: Us nerds can get caught up in the details of how things are built. Like connoisseurs of fine code we can endlessly debate the best way to do something. But at the end of the day, a beautiful piece of code is worthless if it sucks to use.
ControversialOpinions.opinion3Paragraph1: Most enterprise software is designed to be sold, not used. It's packed with features nobody needs, requires months of implementation, and ends up being worked around rather than worked with.
ControversialOpinions.opinion3Paragraph2: Simple tools that do one thing well beat complex platforms that do everything poorly. Your team will actually use them.
ControversialOpinions.opinion4Title: Meetings Are Where Work Goes to Die
ControversialOpinions.opinion4Subtitle: If it could be an email, it should be an email.
ControversialOpinions.opinion4Paragraph1: The default response to any problem in corporate America is to schedule a meeting. Most meetings exist because someone didn't want to make a decision or write something down.
ControversialOpinions.opinion4Paragraph2: We bias heavily toward async communication and written documentation. When we do meet, it's because we need to actually discuss something, not because it's Tuesday at 10am.
ControversialOpinions.opinion5Title: Perfect Is the Enemy of Done
ControversialOpinions.opinion5Paragraph1: We've seen too many projects die in pursuit of perfection. Six months of planning, endless stakeholder reviews, and comprehensive documentation—followed by a launch that flops because nobody actually used the thing until it was "ready".
ControversialOpinions.opinion5Paragraph2: We'd rather ship something rough in two weeks, learn from real usage, and iterate. You'll end up with a better product faster, and you'll waste less money on features nobody wanted.
ControversialOpinions.opinion6Paragraph1: Best practices are usually just "practices that worked for someone else in a different context." Blindly following them without understanding why they exist leads to cargo cult engineering.
ControversialOpinions.opinion6Paragraph2: We think from first principles. Sometimes that means following conventions. Sometimes it means ignoring them entirely. The goal is solving your problem, not checking boxes.
ControversialOpinions.ctaDescription: We'd love to hear your take. Let's have a conversation.
